title: The Hero in the Age of Checklists
coreMove: Redefine professional excellence so shared verification counts as strength rather than insult.
sourcePressure: The source turns to resistance to checklist adoption, ego, professional identity, lone-hero mythology, and the need for disciplined teamwork in complex work.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version mocks experts for arrogance. The real chapter shows why a proven tool can still threaten the way professionals understand competence.

sourceAnchors.name: resistance to checklist adoption
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar says this chapter turns to resistance to checklist adoption after evidence exists.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Resistance survives proof because the list is asking professionals to change the public shape of competence.

sourceAnchors.name: lone-hero mythology
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar identifies lone-hero mythology and teamwork as the chapter's professional identity conflict.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The lone hero looks brave on the poster and brittle in a crowded operating room.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Grace, a cardiac surgery fellow leading timeout adoption
exampleSpecs.audience: high-skill teams where hierarchy makes verification feel embarrassing
exampleSpecs.stakes: a senior surgeon sees the timeout as an insult and the junior team goes silent
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Grace frames the timeout as a team reliability act and asks the senior surgeon to answer the same identity and antibiotic checks as everyone else
exampleSpecs.firstImage: the snap of sterile gloves in a room that has gone quiet

exampleSpecs.domain: Olivier, a law firm partner debating a closing checklist
exampleSpecs.audience: elite professionals who equate verification with junior work
exampleSpecs.stakes: a financing close depends on signatures, wire instructions, and filing windows that partners assume associates handle
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Olivier stops calling the list administrative and signs the same final verification line before the wire release
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "I did not spend twenty years to read boxes," Olivier says beside the closing binder

exampleSpecs.domain: Hannah, an orchestra tour manager managing load-in
exampleSpecs.audience: arts leaders coordinating expert performers and technical crews
exampleSpecs.stakes: a principal musician resents equipment checks until the missing case threatens the evening performance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hannah makes the soloist verify instrument, case tag, and stage position with crew instead of treating the check as beneath artistry
exampleSpecs.firstImage: black instrument cases lined like dominoes behind the concert hall

exampleSpecs.domain: Pavel, an emergency department attending during senior surgeon handoff
exampleSpecs.audience: clinical leaders who need status to bend toward team reliability
exampleSpecs.stakes: a high-status consultant skips the handoff pause and leaves blood type verification vague
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Pavel chooses to make the consultant repeat the shared verification in front of the team rather than privately patching the gap
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 1:27 a.m., Pavel sees the trauma bay doors swing open behind the consultant

exampleSpecs.domain: Isabel, an aviation maintenance supervisor changing signoff culture
exampleSpecs.audience: maintenance teams where senior mechanics rely on reputation
exampleSpecs.stakes: a veteran mechanic views a second signoff as distrust after twenty years on the line
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Isabel moves the second signoff from a suspicion ritual to a shared standard every mechanic uses on critical fasteners
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You watch a veteran place his torque wrench down without looking at the second-signoff slot

exampleSpecs.domain: Min, a mountain rescue rope-team leader
exampleSpecs.audience: rescue teams whose identity prizes toughness and improvisation
exampleSpecs.stakes: a rope-team knot check feels like novice theater until fatigue and darkness raise the cost of pride
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Min asks the fastest climber to lead the knot callout and makes public verification part of elite behavior
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Who has enough skill to say the knot out loud?

skillTargets: separate evidence resistance from identity resistance
evaluate adoption moves that preserve dignity and reliability

tryThisNowSpec: Name one verification you avoid because it feels beneath your skill, then decide how to make it a team standard rather than a personal confession.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
